Sliding window
text: A range over a sequence that moves forward, updated by adding what enters and removing what leaves instead of recomputing from scratch.

title: Fixed window
text: A window whose size never changes. Each step, one item enters on the right and exactly one leaves on the left.

title: Variable window
text: A window that grows on the right while it stays valid and shrinks on the left when it breaks a rule, such as 'at most k surges'.

title: Monotonic deque
text: A double-ended queue kept in sorted order by popping values that can never win again. It gives the max or min of a sliding window in O(1) per step.

title: Amortised cost
text: The average cost per operation over a whole run. An inner loop can be fine if, across the run, each item enters and leaves at most once.

title: Two pointers
text: Two indices that move through a sequence by rules, so each position is visited a small number of times. A sliding window is two pointers that bound a range.

title: Hash map
text: A key–value table with O(1) average lookup. In window problems it remembers counts or the last position of each item.

title: Machine coding
text: An interview round where you build a small working system in 60 to 120 minutes: clean classes, a runnable demo, and an extra requirement the interviewer adds partway through.

title: Strategy pattern
text: Each variant of a behaviour (equal, exact or percentage split) lives in its own class behind one interface, so adding a variant means adding a class, not editing a growing if/else.

title: Service layer
text: The class that holds the use cases (add an expense, settle up). It validates input, coordinates the entities and storage, and is the API the interviewer calls.

title: Netting
text: Keeping one signed balance per pair instead of a list of debts: A owes B ₹200 and B owes A ₹50 becomes A owes B ₹150.

title: Back-of-the-envelope estimate
text: Quick arithmetic with round numbers (a day is about 10⁵ seconds) to size traffic, storage and machines before choosing a design.

title: Peak factor
text: How much busier the busiest moment is than the average. Systems are sized for the peak: a 10× promo blast, not a quiet Tuesday.

title: Cache-aside
text: The app checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, then stores the result in the cache for next time.

title: Base 62
text: Writing a number with 62 symbols: 0–9, a–z and A–Z. Seven characters cover 62⁷, about 3.5 trillion values.

title: Message queue
text: A durable buffer between the code that produces work and the workers that do it, so slow or failing work (like recording a click) doesn't hold up the request.

title: Allocation rule
text: The exact order in which a system hands out a scarce resource (a slot, a seat, a driver). Writing it down as a precise order makes it testable and easy to change.

title: Eviction policy
text: The rule a full cache uses to choose what to drop. LRU drops whatever was used longest ago; LFU drops whatever was used the fewest times.

title: Token bucket
text: A rate limit as a bucket of tokens that refills at a steady rate up to a capacity. Each request takes one token; an empty bucket means wait. The capacity is the biggest burst allowed.

title: Undo log
sub: Concept · Key-value store with TTL and transactions
text: A record of what each change overwrote, kept while a transaction is open. Rolling back replays it backwards; committing keeps the changes (or hands the log to the transaction outside).

title: Fail open / fail closed
text: What a check does when something it depends on is down. Fail open lets requests through unchecked (stays available); fail closed refuses them (stays safe). The right choice depends on which failure costs more.

title: Idempotency key
text: A unique id attached to a request so that doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. The receiver records ids it has handled and skips repeats, which makes retries safe.

title: Fan-out
text: Copying one event to many recipients. On write, each new post is pushed into every follower's feed; on read, each feed load gathers posts from everyone followed. Big systems mix the two.

title: State machine
text: A design where what an object may do depends on which state it's in, and actions move it between states. The state pattern puts each state's rules in its own object instead of if-chains in every method.

title: Seat hold
text: A short lease on a scarce item (a seat, a room, stock) while the customer pays. It's taken all at once or not at all, and it ends on its own when time runs out.

title: SCAN (the elevator algorithm)
text: Serve requests by sweeping in one direction while any lie ahead, then reversing. Fair and simple: nobody waits more than about two sweeps. Also used to schedule disk heads.

title: Price-time priority
text: How an exchange decides who trades first: the best price wins, and among orders at the same price, the one that arrived first. Trades happen at the price of the order that was already resting.

title: Virtual waiting room
text: A line in front of a system that can't serve everyone at once. Each arrival gets a number from one shared counter, and fans are admitted in order at a rate the system can safely take; everyone else sees their place.

title: WebSocket
text: A connection a client opens once and keeps open, so either side can send at any time. Servers can push messages instantly instead of waiting to be asked; the cost is holding millions of open connections.

title: Idempotency key
text: A unique id the client sends with a request and every retry of it. The server stores it with the result (under a unique constraint), so a repeat returns the first result instead of doing the work, or charging the card, again.
